terms: The controller is responsible for complying with the data protection principles and must be able to prove it, using suitable technical and organisational measures.
Personal data must be accurate and, where necessary, kept up to date. Every reasonable step must be taken to erase or correct inaccurate data without delay.
A European Commission decision that a non-EU country, territory, sector or international organisation protects personal data adequately. Data can then flow there without specific authorisation.

A money penalty a data protection authority can impose for GDPR infringements. It must be effective, proportionate and dissuasive; the highest tier is up to 20 million euro or 4% of worldwide annual turnover, if higher.

The EU law on artificial intelligence. It bans some AI practices, sets requirements for high-risk AI systems and rules for general-purpose AI models. It was amended in 2026 by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744.
The skills, knowledge and understanding that let providers, deployers and affected people use AI systems in an informed way and be aware of AI's opportunities, risks and possible harms.
The European Commission's function for implementing, monitoring and supervising AI systems, general-purpose AI models and AI governance. References to the AI Office in the AI Act mean the Commission.
A controlled framework set up by an authority where providers can develop, train, validate and test an innovative AI system for a limited time under regulatory supervision.

A machine-based system that works with some autonomy and works out, from the input it receives, how to produce outputs such as predictions, content, recommendations or decisions that can affect physical or virtual environments.
Information that does not relate to an identifiable person, or data made anonymous so that no one can identify the person by any means reasonably likely to be used. The GDPR does not apply to it.

Without an adequacy decision, data may go outside the EU only with appropriate safeguards, such as standard contractual clauses or binding corporate rules, and with enforceable rights and effective remedies for people.

The advisory group of national data protection authorities set up under the 1995 Data Protection Directive. It published influential opinions and guidelines until the GDPR replaced it with the European Data Protection Board in May 2018.
A person or company in the EU with a written mandate from an AI provider to carry out the provider's AI Act obligations and procedures on its behalf.
Automated decision-making|Automated Processing|Right Not To Be Subject to Fully Automated Decisions|Right To Object to Automated Decision-Making

People have the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions, including profiling, with legal or similarly significant effects, unless needed for a contract, allowed by law, or based on explicit consent.
Behavioral Advertising|Online Behavioral Advertising|Retargeting|Remarketing|Psychographic Advertising|Demographic Advertising|Contextual Advertising

Advertising based on watching people's behaviour over time, such as sites visited, to build a profile and show ads matching their inferred interests. The Court of Justice held that Facebook users cannot reasonably expect it without consent.
Internal data protection policies that a group of companies, or companies in a joint economic activity, follow so they can transfer personal data to their members outside the EU.

An AI system that sorts people into specific categories based on their biometric data, unless this is a minor part of another commercial service and strictly necessary for objective technical reasons.

Personal data produced by specific technical processing of a person's physical, physiological or behavioural characteristics, such as facial images or fingerprints. The GDPR version adds that they allow or confirm unique identification.

Facial recognition technology processes biometric data, so it involves special categories of personal data. Processing biometric data to uniquely identify someone is banned unless a GDPR Article 9 exception applies.
Automated recognition of human physical, physiological, behavioural or psychological features to establish a person's identity by comparing their biometric data with stored biometric data.
Automated one-to-one check, including authentication, that a person is who they claim to be, by comparing their biometric data with biometric data they provided before.

Combining a set of information elements to uniquely identify a particular device or app. EU regulators say the ePrivacy rule on accessing device information, which requires consent unless an exemption applies, covers it.
A connection made through a public interpersonal communications service that allows two-way voice communication.
The marking by which a provider shows that an AI system meets the AI Act's high-risk requirements and other applicable EU laws that require the marking.
Certificates, seals and marks that show that processing complies with the GDPR. A certificate does not reduce the controller's or processor's own responsibility.
Charter of Fundamental Rights|Charter Rights|Right to Privacy, The|Privacy|Information Privacy|Data Protection

The EU's bill of rights. Article 7 protects private life and communications; Article 8 makes protection of personal data a separate right, overseen by independent authorities. It has the same legal value as the EU Treaties.

AI systems such as ChatGPT built on large language models, a kind of deep learning model. The GDPR accuracy principle applies to their outputs, and people must be told when they are interacting with an AI system.

Churches and religious bodies that already had comprehensive data protection rules when the GDPR entered into force may keep them if brought into line with the GDPR, under an independent, possibly church-specific, supervisory authority.

Using IT services, such as storage or software, provided over the internet. When a provider processes personal data for a customer, the customer may only use providers giving sufficient guarantees of GDPR compliance.
Codes of Conduct|Co-regulatory Model|Self-Regulation Model, The
Rulebooks, which associations and other bodies representing controllers or processors may prepare, that specify how the GDPR applies in their sector. Authorities and the Commission encourage them.
A set of technical specifications that gives a way to comply with certain AI Act requirements, as defined in Regulation (EU) No 1025/2012.

Any information exchanged between a limited number of parties through a public electronic communications service. Broadcasting to the public is excluded unless linked to an identifiable subscriber or user.

Using personal data for a new purpose is allowed only if it is compatible with the original one. The controller weighs the link between the purposes, the context, the kind of data, the consequences and the safeguards.

Public authorities, or other bodies given public powers by national law, that prevent, investigate, detect or prosecute crime or enforce criminal penalties. The GDPR does not cover their processing for these purposes.
Conditions applicable to a child's consent

For online services offered directly to children and based on consent, a child can consent alone from 16. Below that, a parent must give or authorise consent. EU countries may lower the age, but not below 13.

EU countries must protect the confidentiality of communications and traffic data on public networks. Listening, tapping, storing or other interception by anyone other than the users is banned without their consent, unless legally authorised.
The process of showing whether a high-risk AI system meets the AI Act's requirements for high-risk systems.
A body that carries out independent third-party conformity assessment, including testing, certification and inspection.
A person's freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous agreement to the processing of their data, given by a clear statement or a clear positive action.
The procedures through which data protection authorities cooperate with each other, and where relevant with the European Commission, so that the GDPR is applied consistently across the EU.
The person, company, authority or other body that decides, alone or with others, why and how personal data are processed.
The Council of Europe's 1981 treaty on data protection. Unlike the GDPR, countries outside Europe can join it. A 2018 amending protocol updates it; the updated version is known as 'Convention 108+'.
Cookie (storing or accessing information on a terminal device)
Cookie|Cookie Directive|Local Shared Objects|Flash|Super Cookie|Persistent Storage|Transient Storage

Storing information, such as a cookie, on a user's device, or reading information already stored there, is allowed only with the user's consent after clear and comprehensive information, unless an exemption applies.

A cookie wall blocks access unless the user accepts cookies; the EDPB says such consent is not freely given. Most authorities see a consent banner with no reject option on any layer as an infringement.
The powers a data protection authority has to act on infringements, including warnings, reprimands, temporary or permanent limits on processing such as a ban, and fines.
A human rights organisation of European states, based in Strasbourg and separate from the EU. It created the European Convention on Human Rights and Convention 108 on data protection.

The EU institution where government ministers of the Member States meet. Together with the European Parliament it adopts EU laws such as the GDPR. Not to be confused with the European Council or the Council of Europe.
Court of Justice of the European Union
Court of Justice of the European Union
The EU's court system in Luxembourg. National courts ask it how EU law, including the GDPR, must be interpreted, and its answers bind courts and regulators across the EU.
CJEU C-634/21 SCHUFA Holding, operative part
Calculating a score of how likely someone is to repay. The Court of Justice held that a credit agency's automated score is an automated decision under Article 22 when a lender relies strongly on it.
Under the AI Act, critical infrastructure as defined in Directive (EU) 2022/2557 on the resilience of critical entities.
Processing that takes place through a company's establishments in more than one EU country, or through one establishment but substantially affecting people in more than one EU country.

Interface designs that push users into unintended decisions, often against their interests, such as about their personal data. The Digital Services Act bans them on online platforms, except where the GDPR or consumer law applies.

The EU law on who may access and use data generated by connected products and related services. Users get rights to their device data and can switch cloud services more easily. The GDPR still applies to personal data.

Companies that collect personal data from many sources and sell or share it with others. Because they rarely get the data from the people themselves, GDPR Article 14 requires them to inform those people.
Personal data about a person's physical or mental health, including the health care services they receive, that reveal information about their health status.
Health data and other sensitive data may be processed for research, archiving or statistics if EU or national law allows it, proportionately and with specific safeguards for the people concerned.

The EU law on sharing data: re-use of protected data held by public bodies, trusted data intermediaries, and 'data altruism' organisations that collect data people donate for general-interest purposes.
Data Minimization Principle|Collection Limitation|Data Minimisation Principle
Only personal data that are adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary for the purpose may be processed.
The binding contract or other legal act between a controller and a processor that sets out what is processed, why, for how long, and the parties' obligations and rights.
Data protection by design and by default
Data Protection by Design|Data Protection by Default|Privacy by Design|Privacy engineering|Privacy-Enhancing Technologies|Value-Sensitive Design
Controllers must build data protection into their systems from the design stage, and set defaults so that only the personal data needed for each specific purpose are processed.
Data Protection Directive|EU Data Protection Directive
The EU's data protection law before the GDPR. As a directive it had to be turned into national law, which led to different rules from country to country. The GDPR repealed it on 25 May 2018.
Data Protection Impact Assessment|Privacy Impact Assessment|PIA Triggers|Privacy Threshold Analysis|Privacy Risk
An assessment a controller must carry out before starting processing that is likely to result in a high risk to people's rights and freedoms, especially when new technologies are used.
Data Protection Officer|Privacy Officer|Chief Privacy Officer

An independent expert who advises on and monitors GDPR compliance. Public bodies must appoint one, as must organisations whose core work involves large-scale monitoring of people or large-scale sensitive data.
Data Retention Directive|EU Data Retention Directive
CJEU C-293/12 Digital Rights Ireland and Others, operative part

Laws requiring telecoms providers to keep traffic and location data. The Court of Justice declared the EU Data Retention Directive invalid and precludes general, indiscriminate preventive retention, with exceptions such as serious threats to national security.
The individual whom personal data are about, whether already identified or identifiable.
AI-generated or AI-manipulated image, audio or video that resembles real people, objects, places or events and would falsely appear authentic or truthful to a person.
Anyone who uses an AI system under its own authority, except a person using it for a personal, non-professional activity.
Exceptions that allow a transfer outside the EU without an adequacy decision or safeguards, in specific situations such as the person's explicit consent after being told the risks.
The EU law that sets obligations for 'gatekeepers', the largest digital platforms. Among other things it limits how they combine users' personal data across their services without consent.

The EU law on online intermediaries such as hosting services and online platforms. It sets rules on illegal content, transparency and advertising, with extra duties for very large platforms and search engines.

People can object at any time to the use of their data for direct marketing, including related profiling, and the data must then no longer be used for it. Such processing may be based on legitimate interests.
When data protection authorities disagree on a case, for example over an objection to the lead authority's draft decision, the European Data Protection Board settles it with a binding decision.
Anyone in the supply chain, other than the provider or the importer, who makes an AI system available on the EU market.
Do not track and browser signals
For online services, people may exercise their right to object by automated technical means, such as a browser signal.
A provider of an AI system that builds in an AI model, whether the model is its own or supplied by another company under a contract.
The transmission systems and equipment that carry signals by wire, radio, optical or other electromagnetic means, including satellite, fixed (including internet) and mobile networks.

A service normally provided for payment over electronic networks: internet access, interpersonal communications such as calls and messaging, and signal transmission. Services that provide or edit the content itself are excluded.
Any text, voice, sound or image message sent over a public communications network that can be stored in the network or on the recipient's device until the recipient collects it.
An AI system that identifies or infers people's emotions or intentions from their biometric data.

EU countries may set more specific rules, by law or collective agreement, to protect workers' personal data in the employment context, for example in recruitment and in carrying out the employment contract.
Bring Your Own Device|Background Screening/Checks|Corporate Owned, Personally Enabled (COPE)

An employer monitoring its staff. National rules on employee data must protect workers' dignity and rights, including for workplace monitoring systems, and consent is rarely valid because employees depend on their employer.

Encryption|Asymmetric Encryption|Symmetric Key Encryption|Cryptography|Ciphertext|Encryption Key|Public Key Infrastructure|Storage Encryption|Network Encryption|Transport Layer Security|Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure

A way to make data unintelligible to anyone not authorised to access them. The GDPR names it as a security measure, and if breached data were encrypted the controller need not inform the people affected.
Any person or organisation carrying on an economic activity, whatever its legal form, including partnerships and associations that regularly do so.
ePrivacy Directive|Directive on Privacy and Electronic Communications Act 2002/58EC

The EU law on privacy in electronic communications. It covers the confidentiality of communications, traffic and location data, cookies and similar tracking, and unsolicited marketing by email, text or phone.

A real and effective activity in the EU carried out through stable arrangements, whatever their legal form. According to the EDPB, even one employee or agent can be enough if they act with sufficient stability.
The data protection law for the EU's own institutions, bodies, offices and agencies, mirroring the GDPR. The European Data Protection Supervisor enforces it.

The current EU adequacy decision for the United States, adopted on 10 July 2023 after Schrems II. Personal data can flow freely to US organisations that have signed up and appear on the Data Privacy Framework List.
The 2016 successor to Safe Harbor for sending personal data to certified US companies. The EU Court of Justice declared it invalid in July 2020 (Schrems II) because of US surveillance law.

A board of one representative per Member State that advises the Commission and national authorities so that the AI Act is applied consistently. The European Data Protection Supervisor takes part as an observer.
The EU's executive. It proposes new EU laws, checks that Member States apply EU law, and adopts decisions such as findings that a non-EU country protects personal data adequately.

The Council of Europe's human rights treaty of 1950. Its Article 8 protects private and family life, home and correspondence, and the European Court of Human Rights has read it to cover personal data.
The meeting of the EU's heads of state or government. It sets the EU's overall political direction but does not pass laws.
The Council of Europe's court in Strasbourg. It decides complaints that a state has breached the European Convention on Human Rights, including the right to private life in Article 8.
European Data Protection Board|Opinions of the Article 29 Working Party

The EU body that brings together the national data protection authorities and the European Data Protection Supervisor. It issues guidelines and binding decisions so that the GDPR is applied the same way everywhere.
The independent authority that supervises how the EU's own institutions and bodies handle personal data. It is also a member of the European Data Protection Board.
The EU Member States plus Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway, which share the EU single market. The GDPR was incorporated into the EEA Agreement in 2018, so it applies in those three countries too.
The EU law regulating telecoms networks and services. Its definition of 'electronic communications service' decides which services, including some messaging apps, fall under the ePrivacy Directive.
European Parliament|Members of the European Parliament
The directly elected parliament of the EU. Together with the Council it adopts EU laws, including the GDPR and the AI Act.
A stricter form of consent, used for example to lift the ban on processing sensitive data: the person must expressly state their agreement, for instance in writing.
Any organised set of personal data that can be searched by specific criteria, whether it is kept in one place or spread out.
Any mathematical operation involving floating-point numbers. The AI Act uses the number of these operations used to train a general-purpose AI model to presume it has high-impact capabilities.
Consent counts only if the person has a real choice. It is doubtful when a service is made conditional on consent to processing it does not need, or when there is a clear imbalance of power.

An assessment of the impact on fundamental rights that certain deployers of high-risk AI systems, such as public bodies and private providers of public services, must carry out before using the system.

The EU's main data protection law, applying since 25 May 2018. Fines for the most serious breaches can reach 20 million euros or, for a company, 4% of its worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher.

An AI model, including one trained on large amounts of data, that is very general, performs a wide range of tasks competently and can be built into many systems. Research and prototype models are excluded.
General-purpose AI model with systemic risk

A general-purpose AI model with high-impact capabilities, or one the Commission decides is equivalent. Training with more than 10 to the power of 25 floating-point operations triggers a presumption of high-impact capabilities.
An AI system built on a general-purpose AI model that can serve many purposes, either directly or as part of other AI systems.
Personal data about a person's inherited or acquired genetic characteristics that give unique information about their physiology or health, in particular from analysing a biological sample.
A controlling company together with the companies it controls.
A European standard adopted at the request of the European Commission for applying EU harmonisation legislation.
Capabilities that match or exceed those of the most advanced general-purpose AI models.
An AI system that is, or is a safety component of, a product needing third-party checks under EU product laws, or an AI system listed in Annex III, unless it poses no significant risk of harm.
Household exemption (purely personal or household activity)
The GDPR does not apply to individuals processing data for purely personal or household purposes, such as private letters or address books. It still applies to companies that provide the tools.
High-risk AI systems must be designed so that people can effectively oversee them while they are in use, to prevent or minimise risks to health, safety or fundamental rights.
A person or company in the EU that places on the market an AI system bearing the name or trademark of someone established outside the EU.
A service normally provided for payment, at a distance, by electronic means and at the individual request of the person receiving it, as defined in Directive (EU) 2015/1535.
A test subject's freely given, specific, unambiguous and voluntary agreement to take part in real-world testing, after being told everything relevant to that decision.
Data given to, or directly picked up by, an AI system, from which the system produces an output.
The information a provider gives deployers about an AI system, in particular its intended purpose and proper use.
Personal data must be kept appropriately secure, protected against unauthorised or unlawful use and against accidental loss, destruction or damage, by suitable technical or organisational measures.
The use the provider intends for an AI system, including the specific context and conditions of use, as stated in its instructions, marketing and technical documentation.
An organisation governed by public international law, or any body set up by an agreement between two or more countries.
Internet of Things and connected devices

Devices that produce information continuously, for example through built-in sensors, and share it over networks. Regulators treat connected devices such as cars as terminal equipment, so the ePrivacy rules on accessing device information can apply.
Internet Protocol Address|Media Access Control Address

An IP address can be personal data. Under the GDPR's predecessor, the Court of Justice held that a dynamic IP address is personal data for a website operator legally able to identify the user via the internet provider.
Two or more controllers who decide together why and how data are processed. They must agree who does what, but people can still exercise their rights against each of them.
Investigations and enforcement actions that data protection authorities from several EU countries carry out together.
Activities by or for law enforcement authorities to prevent, investigate, detect or prosecute crime or enforce criminal penalties, including protecting against threats to public security.
Any public authority competent to prevent, investigate, detect or prosecute crime or enforce criminal penalties, or any other body given those public powers by national law.
The GDPR's sister law for police, prosecutors and other authorities handling personal data to fight crime. Member States must turn it into national law.
Legal Basis for Processing|Legitimate Processing Criteria
Processing is lawful only if at least one of six grounds applies: consent, a contract, a legal obligation, vital interests, a task in the public interest, or legitimate interests.
Personal data must be processed lawfully, fairly and in a way that is transparent to the person they are about.
Lead supervisory authority and one-stop shop
For cross-border processing, the authority of the country where a company has its main or single EU establishment leads the case and is the company's only contact point: the one-stop shop.
Processing is lawful if it is necessary to comply with a legal obligation on the controller, laid down in EU or national law.

Processing is lawful if necessary for a legitimate interest of the controller or a third party, unless the person's interests or rights override it, especially for a child. Public authorities cannot use it for their tasks.
Data processed in a communications network or service that show where a user's device, such as a phone, is located.

Information about where a device, and so its user, is. Under the ePrivacy Directive, telecoms location data other than traffic data may only be processed anonymously or with consent for a value added service.
Machine learning and AI training data

Machine learning lets AI systems learn from training data. High-risk systems need quality training data under the AI Act, and the EDPB says models trained on personal data are not automatically anonymous.
For a controller with offices in several EU countries, normally its EU head office, unless another office makes the decisions on why and how data are processed. A separate rule applies to processors.
Supplying an AI system or general-purpose AI model for distribution or use on the EU market as part of a business, whether paid or free.
The national authority that carries out the activities and takes the measures set out in the EU market surveillance regulation, Regulation (EU) 2019/1020.
The GDPR covers processing of personal data by automated means, and manual processing of data that are or will be part of a filing system. Article 2(2) lists the exclusions.

Data about a communication rather than its content: source, destination, date, time, duration, type, equipment and location. The Court of Justice found that, taken together, they can reveal very precise details of private life.
In the AI Act, a micro, small or medium-sized enterprise as defined in Commission Recommendation 2003/361/EC.
Data protection authorities must share relevant information and help each other so the GDPR is applied consistently.
A national notifying authority or market surveillance authority. For AI used by EU institutions and bodies, the European Data Protection Supervisor takes this role.
Each Member State's own data protection law, such as Germany's Federal Data Protection Act (BDSG). It applies alongside the GDPR and fills in the points the GDPR leaves to national law.
EU countries may set specific conditions for processing national identification numbers or similar general identifiers, which may only be used with appropriate safeguards for people's rights.
A limit on a fundamental right is valid only if set by law, respects the right's essence, and is necessary and proportionate to a general interest recognised by the EU or to protect others' rights.
The EU cybersecurity law for important sectors such as energy, transport, health and digital infrastructure. Covered organisations must manage cyber risks and report significant incidents.
Any data that are not personal data as the GDPR defines them.
Notification of a personal data breach

A controller must report a personal data breach to the data protection authority within 72 hours where feasible, unless it is unlikely to create a risk, and must tell the people affected if the risk is high.
A conformity assessment body that has been officially notified under the AI Act and other relevant EU product safety laws.
The national authority that sets up and runs the procedures for assessing, designating and notifying conformity assessment bodies, and for monitoring them.
The umbrella word in the AI Act for a provider, product manufacturer, deployer, authorised representative, importer or distributor.

Processing is lawful if necessary to perform a contract with the person, or to take steps they request before one. The Court of Justice requires it to be objectively indispensable to the contract's main purpose.
How well an AI system achieves its intended purpose.

Any information about an identified or identifiable human being, meaning someone who can be identified directly or indirectly, for example through a name, an ID number, location data or an online identifier.
A security failure that leads to personal data being destroyed, lost, altered, disclosed or accessed without authorisation, whether by accident or unlawfully.
Personal data relating to criminal convictions and offences

Data on criminal convictions and offences may be processed only under official authority control or where EU or national law allows it with appropriate safeguards. Comprehensive criminal records registers must be kept by official authorities.
The first time an AI system or general-purpose AI model is made available on the EU market.
Everything providers do to collect and review experience from AI systems they have put on the market, to spot any need for corrective or preventive action straight away.
Any remote biometric identification system that is not real-time, for example one used on recorded footage.
Principles relating to processing of personal data
Data Protection Principles|Fair Information Practice Principles|OECD Guidelines

The seven core rules for all processing of personal data: lawfulness, fairness and transparency; purpose limitation; data minimisation; accuracy; storage limitation; integrity and confidentiality; and accountability.
If a data protection impact assessment shows that processing would be high risk without mitigating measures, the controller must consult the data protection authority before starting.
Anything done with personal data, by computer or by hand: collecting, recording, storing, changing, looking up, using, sharing, combining, restricting, erasing or destroying it.
Processing and freedom of expression and information (journalism)
EU countries must balance data protection with freedom of expression and information by law, including exemptions for journalism and academic, artistic or literary expression where necessary.
Processing which does not require identification
If a controller does not need to identify the people its data are about, it does not have to collect or keep extra information just to identify them for GDPR purposes.
A person, company, authority or other body that processes personal data on behalf of a controller.

EU countries may adapt the investigative powers of data protection authorities over people bound by professional secrecy, where necessary and proportionate to reconcile data protection with that secrecy.

Automated use of personal data to evaluate aspects of a person, especially to analyse or predict things like their work performance, finances, health, preferences, interests, reliability, behaviour, location or movements.

AI uses that the AI Act bans outright. Under conditions set in Article 5 they include manipulative or deceptive techniques, AI that makes intimate images of identifiable people without consent, and untargeted scraping of facial images.
Whoever develops an AI system or general-purpose AI model, or has one developed, and places it on the market or puts the system into service under its own name or trademark, paid or free.
Processing personal data so that they can no longer be linked to a specific person without extra information, which is kept separately and protected so that the person is not identified.

Data that have been pseudonymised. They stay personal data for anyone who can re-link them to a person with additional information; the Court of Justice held in 2025 this is not automatically so for everyone.
Public bodies may disclose personal data in official documents under EU or national law, to balance public access to documents with data protection.
Public task (public interest or official authority)
Processing is lawful if it is necessary for a task in the public interest or for exercising official authority given to the controller, with a basis in EU or national law.
Any physical place, public or privately owned, that an undetermined number of people can enter, even if conditions or capacity limits apply.
Purpose Limitation|Purpose Specification|Use Limitation|Limiting Use|Identifying Purposes|Repurposing|Secondary use

Personal data may only be collected for specified, explicit and legitimate purposes and not used later in a way that is incompatible with them. Archiving, research and statistics under Article 89(1) count as compatible.
Supplying an AI system for first use directly to the deployer, or for the provider's own use, in the EU for its intended purpose.
Programmatic Buying|Ad Exchange|Ad Network|Demand Side Platform (DSP)|Supply Side Platform (SSP)
An instant, automated online auction in which advertising companies bid, behind the scenes, for ad space on the page a user is viewing, so they can show ads tailored to that user's profile.
A remote biometric identification system where capture, comparison and identification happen without significant delay, including short delays added to prevent the rule being circumvented.
A document setting out the objectives, method, scope, monitoring, organisation and conduct of testing an AI system in real-world conditions.
Using an AI system in a way that departs from its intended purpose but that may result from reasonably foreseeable human behaviour or interaction with other systems.
Any measure to get an AI system that has already been made available to deployers returned to the provider, taken out of service or disabled.
Anyone to whom personal data are disclosed, whether a third party or not. Public authorities receiving data for a particular inquiry under EU or national law do not count as recipients.

Controllers, and processors for their part, must keep a written record of their processing activities. Organisations with fewer than 250 staff are exempt unless the processing is risky, regular or involves sensitive data.

A formal objection by a data protection authority to another authority's draft decision, which must clearly show how the draft creates significant risks for people's rights or for the free flow of data.
An AI system that identifies people without their active involvement, typically at a distance, by comparing their biometric data with a reference database.
People can mandate a not-for-profit body active in data protection to complain, go to court and, where national law allows, claim compensation for them.
A person or company in the EU, appointed in writing by a controller or processor based outside the EU, to represent it for its GDPR obligations.
Representative of a controller not established in the EU

Controllers and processors outside the EU that target people in the EU must appoint an EU representative in writing, except public bodies and occasional, low-risk processing without large-scale sensitive or criminal data.
A formal statement by a data protection authority that a controller's or processor's processing has infringed the GDPR. It is one of the authority's corrective powers.
Processing for archiving in the public interest, research or statistics must have appropriate safeguards, such as measures ensuring data minimisation, which may include pseudonymisation.
Marking stored personal data so that they are only used in limited ways in the future.

EU or national law may limit data subjects' rights and some related duties, but only by legislation that respects the essence of fundamental rights and is necessary and proportionate to protect interests the GDPR lists.
Right of Access|Individual Access|Customer Access|Individual Participation
People can ask a controller whether it processes their personal data and, if so, get access to the data, a copy, and information about the processing.
Right to an effective judicial remedy
The right to go to court against a binding decision of a data protection authority, and against a controller or processor that infringed one's GDPR rights.
Anyone who suffers material or non-material damage because of a GDPR infringement can claim compensation from the controller or processor, unless it proves it was in no way responsible.
People can get the personal data they gave a controller in a structured, machine-readable format and pass them to another controller, where processing is automated and based on consent or a contract.
Right to erasure ('right to be forgotten')

People can have their personal data erased without undue delay in listed cases, for example when the data are no longer needed or consent is withdrawn. Exceptions include freedom of expression and legal obligations.
Anyone who thinks the processing of their data breaks the GDPR can complain to a data protection authority, in particular in the country where they live or work, or where the infringement happened.

People can object to processing based on public task or legitimate interests, for reasons linked to their situation; the controller must stop unless it shows compelling grounds. Objection to direct marketing always succeeds.
People can have inaccurate personal data about them corrected without undue delay, and incomplete data completed.
People can require a controller to limit the use of their data in listed cases, for example while the accuracy of the data is being checked.
Under the AI Act, how likely harm is to happen combined with how serious that harm would be.

The 2000 arrangement under which US companies could receive EU personal data by signing up to privacy principles. The EU Court of Justice declared the Commission's decision invalid in October 2015 (Schrems I).
A part of a product or AI system that fulfils a safety function, or whose failure would endanger people's health and safety or property.
A document agreed between the provider and the competent authority describing the objectives, conditions, timeframe, method and requirements for activities in an AI regulatory sandbox.
Appropriate Technical and Organizational Measures|Information Security|Security Policy|Resilience|Encryption|Multi-Factor Authentication|Least Privilege|Role-Based Access Controls

Controllers and processors must protect personal data with technical and organisational measures suited to the risk, such as pseudonymisation, encryption and keeping systems confidential, intact, available and resilient.
Operational data from crime prevention, detection, investigation or prosecution work whose disclosure could put criminal proceedings at risk.

An AI incident or malfunction that directly or indirectly leads to death or serious harm to health, serious disruption of critical infrastructure, breach of EU fundamental-rights duties, or serious harm to property or the environment.
A company that is not an SME, employs fewer than 750 people and has a yearly turnover of at most 150 million euro or a balance sheet total of at most 129 million euro.

A seller that got a customer's email address in a sale may email them about its own similar products without consent, if the customer can easily object for free when the address is collected and in every message.
Special Categories of Data|Sensitive Personal Information|Medical Information

Sensitive data: racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religious or philosophical beliefs, trade union membership, genetic data, biometric data used for identification, health, sex life or sexual orientation. Processing them is banned unless an exception applies.
Model contract clauses adopted by the European Commission. When the sender and the receiver of data sign them, they count as appropriate safeguards for transfers outside the GDPR's reach.
Personal data must not be kept in a form that identifies people for longer than the purpose of the processing requires.
Cookies that need no consent because they are used only to transmit a communication, or are strictly necessary to provide a service the user explicitly asked for.
Another processor that a processor brings in to help process the data. This needs the controller's prior written authorisation, and the first processor stays fully liable for it.
A change to an AI system after it reaches the market or is put into service, not planned in the original conformity assessment, that affects its compliance or changes its intended purpose.
An independent public authority set up by an EU country to monitor how the GDPR is applied. It is commonly called a data protection authority.
A data protection authority that has a say in a case because the company is established in its country, people in its country are substantially affected, or a complaint was lodged with it.

A risk tied to the high-impact capabilities of general-purpose AI models that can significantly affect the EU market or public health, safety, security, fundamental rights or society, and spread at scale.
Targeting (offering goods or services, monitoring behaviour)
An organisation outside the EU falls under the GDPR if it offers goods or services to people in the EU or monitors their behaviour there. A website merely being reachable from the EU is not enough.

The GDPR applies to organisations established in the EU, wherever the processing happens, and to organisations outside the EU that offer goods or services to people in the EU or monitor their behaviour there.
Data used for an independent evaluation of an AI system, to confirm that it performs as expected before it is placed on the market or put into service.
Temporary testing of an AI system for its intended purpose in the real world, outside a lab. It does not count as placing on the market if the AI Act's conditions are met.
The Treaty article that states the right to data protection and gives the EU the power to adopt data protection laws. The GDPR and the Law Enforcement Directive are based on it.
Six Major European Union Institutions, The|European Union|Member State|European Economic Community|Treaty of Lisbon
The seven bodies the EU Treaties name as the Union's institutions, from the Parliament and the Commission to the Court of Justice. Together they make, apply and interpret EU law.
Anyone other than the data subject, the controller, the processor and the people authorised to process the data under their direct authority.

A link to a resource, usually an image, embedded in a web page or email to make the device contact the pixel's host. The EDPB treats collecting identifiers this way as covered by the ePrivacy rule on device access.
Data processed to carry a communication over an electronic communications network, or to bill for it.
Data used to train an AI system by fitting its learnable parameters.
Transfer impact assessment and supplementary measures

Before relying on a transfer tool such as standard contractual clauses, the exporter checks whether the destination country's law or practice could undermine it, and if so adds measures to keep protection essentially equivalent.
Transfer of personal data to a third country
Personal data may be sent to a country outside the EU or to an international organisation only if the conditions in Chapter V of the GDPR are met, including for onward transfers.
Transparency and information to data subjects
Privacy Notice|Privacy Policy|Layered Notice|Just-in-Time Notification|Standardized Icons|Data Protection Policy
Controllers must tell people about the processing of their data, when the data are collected, in a concise, transparent, intelligible and easily accessible form, using clear and plain language.

People must be told when they are interacting with an AI system, unless it is obvious, and AI-generated audio, images, video and text must be marked as artificially generated in a machine-readable way.
Consent must be shown by a statement or a clear positive action, such as ticking a box. Silence, pre-ticked boxes or doing nothing are not consent.
The human rights declaration proclaimed by the United Nations General Assembly on 10 December 1948. Its Article 12 protects privacy, family, home and correspondence against arbitrary interference.
Unsolicited communications (direct marketing by email, SMS, calls)

Direct marketing by automatic calling machines, fax or electronic mail needs prior consent. For other unsolicited marketing, each EU country chooses between requiring consent and allowing it unless people say they do not want it.

In exceptional, urgent cases, a data protection authority can adopt temporary measures for its own territory straight away, for up to three months, without waiting for the usual cooperation procedures.
Under the ePrivacy Directive, any individual who uses a public electronic communications service, privately or for business, even without being a subscriber.
Data used to evaluate a trained AI system and tune its non-learnable parameters and learning process, for example to prevent underfitting or overfitting.
A separate data set, or a part of the training data set, kept aside for validation.
A service that needs traffic data or location data beyond what is necessary to carry or bill a communication.

Filming people with cameras such as CCTV. The EDPB says it is not necessary by default where other means can achieve the purpose. Large-scale systematic monitoring of public areas requires a data protection impact assessment.

Processing is lawful if it is necessary to protect an interest essential to the life of the person or of someone else. Relying on another person's vital interests should in principle be a last resort.

Reporting breaches of EU law learned at work. The Whistleblower Directive protects people who report, including breaches of data protection law, and reports must themselves be handled in line with the GDPR.
A breach of EU law protecting individuals that harms, or is likely to harm, the collective interests of people in several EU countries, as the AI Act defines in detail.
Any measure to stop an AI system that is in the supply chain from being made available on the market.
People can withdraw their consent at any time, and withdrawing must be as easy as giving it. Processing carried out before the withdrawal remains lawful.
Judgment of 24 November 2011, ASNEF and FECEMD, C-468/10 and C-469/10, EU:C:2011:777, operative part, point 1

Spain could not add a condition that data processed under the legitimate interests ground must come from public sources. Member States cannot narrow that ground with extra rules, and people can rely on it directly in court.
Judgment of 29 June 2010, Bavarian Lager, C-28/08 P, EU:C:2010:378, paragraph 63

When someone asks an EU institution for documents containing personal data, the data protection rules for EU institutions apply in full. The Commission could withhold names of meeting participants because the requester gave no express and legitimate reason for needing them.
Judgment of 19 October 2016, Breyer, C-582/14, EU:C:2016:779, operative part, point 1

A dynamic IP address kept by a website operator is personal data for that operator if it has legal means to identify the person using information held by the internet access provider. National law also cannot rule out weighing the operator's legitimate interests.
Judgment of 5 September 2017, Bărbulescu v. Romania, no. 61496/08, ECLI:CE:ECHR:2017:0905JUD006149608, § 140

A sales engineer was dismissed after his employer read his Yahoo Messenger chats, including private ones. The Grand Chamber found a violation because the national courts did not check whether he had been warned in advance and whether the monitoring was justified and limited.
Judgment of 9 March 2010, Commission v Germany, C-518/07, EU:C:2010:125, paragraph 30

Data protection authorities must be completely independent, free from any outside influence including the state's. Germany broke EU law by placing the regional authorities that supervise private companies under state scrutiny.
Judgment of 3 April 2007, Copland v. the United Kingdom, no. 62617/00, ECLI:CE:ECHR:2007:0403JUD006261700, § 41

A college employee's phone calls, emails and internet use were monitored. The Court held that work emails and internet use are protected by Article 8, and found a violation because no law regulated such monitoring at the time.
Judgment of 5 December 2023, Deutsche Wohnen, C-807/21, EU:C:2023:950, operative part, point 2
A company can be fined under the GDPR without first pinning the breach on a named manager or employee. But a fine is only possible if the company committed the breach intentionally or negligently.
Judgment of 8 April 2014, Digital Rights Ireland, C-293/12 and C-594/12, EU:C:2014:238, operative part

The Court struck down the EU Data Retention Directive, which required telecoms providers to keep everyone's traffic and location data so authorities could use them against serious crime. The interference with privacy and data protection went beyond what was strictly necessary.
Judgment of 27 February 2025, Dun & Bradstreet Austria, C-203/22, EU:C:2025:117, operative part, point 1

A woman refused a mobile phone contract after an automated credit check was entitled to an explanation of the procedure and principles actually used. Where trade secrets or other people's data are involved, the controller must give them to the regulator or court, which decides what she sees.
Durant v Financial Services Authority [2003] EWCA Civ 1746, 8 December 2003, paragraph 28 (Auld LJ)

An English court read 'personal data' narrowly: information must be biographical and focused on the person, so a document that merely mentions someone is not necessarily their personal data. This is a UK ruling on the Data Protection Act 1998, not EU case law; the EU Court of Justice has since taken a wider view (see Nowak).
Judgment of 4 May 2023, F.F. v Österreichische Datenschutzbehörde, C-487/21, EU:C:2023:369, operative part, point 1

The right to a copy of one's data means a faithful and understandable reproduction of all of it. This can include copies of extracts from documents, or whole documents, where that is essential to exercise GDPR rights.
Judgment of 15 June 2021, Facebook Ireland v Gegevensbeschermingsautoriteit, C-645/19, EU:C:2021:483, operative part, point 1

Under the one-stop shop the lead authority normally handles cross-border cases. But another national authority may take a company to court in its own country in the situations where the GDPR lets it act, if it respects the cooperation procedures.
Judgment of 29 July 2019, Fashion ID, C-40/17, EU:C:2019:629, operative part, point 2

An online shop that embedded Facebook's 'Like' button is a joint controller with Facebook for collecting visitors' data and sending it to Facebook, but not for what Facebook does with the data afterwards.
Judgment of 7 July 1989, Gaskin v. the United Kingdom, no. 10454/83, ECLI:CE:ECHR:1989:0707JUD001045483, § 49

A man who grew up in local authority care was refused parts of his care records because some contributors would not consent. The Court found a violation: an independent authority had to be able to decide on access when a contributor did not answer or refused consent.
Judgment of 24 September 2019, GC and Others, C-136/17, EU:C:2019:773, operative part, point 2

The strict rules on sensitive data, and on data about criminal proceedings, also bind search engines when they handle delisting requests. As a rule such links must be removed unless keeping them is strictly necessary for the public's freedom of information.
Judgment of 13 May 2014, Google Spain, C-131/12, EU:C:2014:317, operative part, point 3

A Spanish man wanted Google to stop showing, under his name, 1998 newspaper notices about the auction of his property to recover social security debts. The Court held that a search engine is a controller and can be required to delist such links, the origin of the 'right to be forgotten'.
Judgment of 24 September 2019, Google v CNIL, C-507/17, EU:C:2019:772, operative part

When a search engine grants a 'right to be forgotten' request, EU law requires it to delist the link on its versions for all EU Member States, not worldwide, and to take measures that discourage users in the EU from reaching it.
Judgment of 27 October 2009, Haralambie c. Roumanie (Haralambie v. Romania), no. 21737/03, ECLI:CE:ECHR:2009:1027JUD002173703, dispositif, point 4

A man asked in 2002 to see the file the communist-era secret police (Securitate) had kept on him and was only invited to consult it in 2008. The Court found that the ineffective access procedure breached his right to respect for private life.
Judgment of 16 December 2008, Huber, C-524/06, EU:C:2008:724, operative part, point 1

Germany's central register of foreign EU citizens was lawful only if it held just the data needed to apply residence law. Keeping named records for statistics was not necessary, and a crime-fighting database only for non-German EU citizens was discriminatory.
Judgment of 7 March 2024, IAB Europe, C-604/22, EU:C:2024:214, operative part, point 1

The 'TC String' that records a user's cookie and advertising choices is personal data when it can reasonably be linked to an identifier such as an IP address. IAB Europe, which wrote the rules, can be a joint controller even without access to the data.
Judgment of 10 July 2018, Jehovan todistajat, C-25/17, EU:C:2018:551, operative part, point 3

Notes taken by Jehovah's Witnesses during door-to-door preaching are not a purely personal activity. The religious community is a joint controller with its preaching members, even though it never sees the notes.
Judgment of 4 October 2024, Koninklijke Nederlandse Lawn Tennisbond, C-621/22, EU:C:2024:858, operative part

The Dutch tennis federation gave members' data to sponsors for payment. A purely commercial interest can be a legitimate interest if it is lawful, but the processing must be strictly necessary and not outweighed by the members' rights.
Judgment of 6 November 2003, Lindqvist, C-101/01, EU:C:2003:596, operative part, point 1

Mrs Lindqvist put pages on the internet naming people from her parish, with details such as their jobs, hobbies and one person's foot injury. The Court held this was processing of personal data, including health data, but that uploading data to a site hosted in the EU is not in itself a transfer to a non-EU country.
Judgment of 17 October 2019, López Ribalda and Others v. Spain, nos. 1874/13 and 8567/13, ECLI:CE:ECHR:2019:1017JUD000187413, operative part

Supermarket staff were filmed by hidden cameras after large stock losses. The Grand Chamber found no violation: reasonable suspicion of serious misconduct justified the covert filming here, though the slightest suspicion would not.
Judgment of 9 March 2017, Manni, C-398/15, EU:C:2017:197, operative part

A businessman has no general right to have his name removed from the public companies register. Member States may let people ask, case by case and in exceptional situations, for access to be limited long after the company was dissolved.
Judgment of 4 July 2023, Meta Platforms v Bundeskartellamt, C-252/21, EU:C:2023:537, operative part, point 1

Germany's competition authority could find that Meta's data terms broke the GDPR when examining abuse of dominance, while cooperating with data protection authorities. The Court read the 'contract' and 'legitimate interests' grounds narrowly, and said dominance does not rule out valid consent but weighs on whether it is free.
Judgment of 5 December 2023, Nacionalinis visuomenės sveikatos centras, C-683/21, EU:C:2023:949, operative part, point 2

Lithuania's public health centre, which had a COVID-19 app developed, could be a controller although it processed no data itself. Joint control needs no formal agreement between the parties, and fines require intent or negligence.
Judgment of 20 December 2017, Nowak, C-434/16, EU:C:2017:994, operative part

A trainee accountant asked for his exam script. The Court held that a candidate's written answers and the examiner's comments on them are his personal data, confirming that 'personal data' covers opinions and assessments, not just private facts.
OT v Vyriausioji tarnybinės etikos komisija
Judgment of 1 August 2022, OT v Vyriausioji tarnybinės etikos komisija, C-184/20, EU:C:2022:601, operative part, point 2

Lithuanian law required online publication of officials' declarations of interests, including names of spouses or partners. The Court held this went too far, and that data which indirectly reveal sensitive facts, such as sexual orientation, are special category data.
Judgment of 1 October 2019, Planet49, C-673/17, EU:C:2019:801, operative part, point 1

A pre-ticked checkbox does not give valid consent to cookies. This is so whether or not the cookie data are personal data, and users must be told how long cookies last and whether third parties can access them.
Judgment of 7 May 2009, Rijkeboer, C-553/07, EU:C:2009:293, operative part
The right of access covers who received your data in the past, not just who receives it now. Keeping that record for only one year was too short unless longer storage would be an excessive burden.
Judgment of 11 December 2014, Ryneš, C-212/13, EU:C:2014:2428, operative part
A home security camera that also films a public space, such as the street, is not covered by the household exemption, so data protection law applies to it.
S. and Marper v United Kingdom
Judgment of 4 December 2008, S. and Marper v. the United Kingdom, nos. 30562/04 and 30566/04, ECLI:CE:ECHR:2008:1204JUD003056204, § 125

The police kept the fingerprints, DNA samples and DNA profiles of two people who were never convicted, with no time limit. The Grand Chamber held that keeping such data from everyone suspected but not convicted, without distinction, breached the right to private life.
Judgment of 6 October 2015, Schrems I, C-362/14, EU:C:2015:650, operative part, point 2

After the Snowden revelations, Max Schrems complained about Facebook sending his data to the United States. The Court held that national authorities can examine such complaints despite a Commission adequacy decision, and declared the Safe Harbor decision invalid.
Judgment of 16 July 2020, Schrems II, C-311/18, EU:C:2020:559, operative part, point 5

The Court declared the EU-US Privacy Shield invalid because of US surveillance law. Standard contractual clauses remain valid, but data sent abroad under them must get protection essentially equivalent to EU law, and regulators must stop transfers where it does not.
Judgment of 4 October 2024, Schrems v Meta, C-446/21, EU:C:2024:834, operative part, point 1

Data minimisation stops a social network from gathering and using all personal data, on and off the platform, for targeted advertising without limits of time or type. Speaking publicly about one's sexual orientation does not let the network use other data about it for ads.
Judgment of 7 December 2023, SCHUFA Holding, C-634/21, EU:C:2023:957, operative part

A credit agency's automated score is itself an automated decision under GDPR Article 22 when a lender or other business relies heavily on it to decide whether to enter into, carry out or end a contract with the person.
Judgment of 5 June 2018, Wirtschaftsakademie Schleswig-Holstein, C-210/16, EU:C:2018:388, operative part, point 1

A business that runs a Facebook fan page is a controller, jointly with Facebook, for the data collected about the page's visitors. The German authority could also act against Facebook's German establishment.
Judgment of 4 May 2023, Österreichische Post, C-300/21, EU:C:2023:370, operative part, point 1

A breach of the GDPR does not on its own give a right to compensation: the person must show damage caused by it. But national law cannot require non-material damage, such as distress, to reach a minimum level of seriousness.
